sourceBindings.text: A crop needs more than a bag marked N–P–K. Learn what these three letters stand for, what the nutrients do, how roots take them up, and what the numbers on a fertilizer label actually mean before making a field decision.
Distinguish the three primary mineral macronutrients from other essential nutrients and match N, P and K with their names and common uptake forms.
Explain the roles of N, P and K with an example, state where the simple analogies stop working, and distinguish a nutrient's presence in soil from its availability to roots.
Read the weight percentages on an N–P₂O₅–K₂O label without treating the P₂O₅ and K₂O figures as percentages of elemental P and K.

sourceBindings.text: A pasture manager wants greener leafy growth and asks which of the three primary mineral nutrients most directly supports it.
Choose N and connect it to chlorophyll, proteins and leaf growth.
Check the soil and other limiting conditions before recommending an amount. A green appearance alone is not a full diagnosis.
A nutrient role can guide investigation without becoming an automatic fertilizer prescription.

sourceBindings.text: Part of a maize field has lodged after a windy day. The farmer asks whether the field must lack K.
Explain that K supports water regulation and stem strength, so K availability is a possible factor.
Examine wind exposure, crop variety, disease and other nutrient or management factors; use observations and a soil test before deciding.
A single symptom does not prove one nutrient deficiency.

sourceBindings.text: A 5 kg bag carries a 10–10–10 label.
Keep the sequence N–P₂O₅–K₂O.
Multiply 5 kg by 0.10 for each listed measure: 0.5 kg N, 0.5 kg P₂O₅ equivalent and 0.5 kg K₂O equivalent.
Do not call the latter two quantities 0.5 kg of elemental P and K.
The same numeral can refer to different chemical reporting bases.

sourceBindings.text: Nine cards in three groups: nutrient names, principal functions and indicative symptom descriptions. Match without the key, justify each choice, then receive feedback. Plan about 10 minutes for this sort within the wider 45-minute activity; the diagnosis stations continue in the step “Evidence-based nutrient symptom interpretation”.
Nitrogen (N)
Phosphorus (P)
Potassium (K)
Leafy growth
Early root development
Disease resistance / plant protection (source wording; means supporting normal defences, not immunity)
Yellow V-pattern on lower maize leaves
Purpling in a young plant
Yellowing at the margins of older leaves
This is knowledge practice. Detailed nutrient transport follows in the next step and symptom diagnosis in step 3 of this station. No field diagnosis or fertilizer-application pass is awarded.

sourceBindings.text: essential nutrient
An element a plant requires to complete its normal life cycle.
mineral macronutrient
An essential mineral element required in comparatively large amounts; primary N/P/K and secondary Ca/Mg/S are distinct groups.
availability
The extent to which a nutrient can be supplied to roots in a usable form at the needed time.
soil solution
Water in soil pores containing dissolved substances, including nutrient ions.
oxide equivalent
A standard fertilizer-label reporting basis for P as P₂O₅ and K as K₂O; not a claim that these are the exact molecules roots absorb.

sourceBindings.text: Learner names N, P and K and correctly matches each symbol and common uptake form; distinguishes this primary mineral group from C/H/O, secondary mineral macronutrients and micronutrients.
Pass only when every grouping and match is accurate; direct the learner to the relevant explanation for each error, then allow another attempt.

Learner explains a useful role for each of N, P and K with the pasture or maize example; states at least one limit of the house/protector analogy and explains why nutrient presence in soil does not prove root availability.
Pass when all three roles, an example, an analogy limit and the availability distinction are justified accurately; otherwise targeted review and open retry.
Learner interprets 10–10–10 as N–P₂O₅–K₂O weight percentages, calculates the three labelled measures for a 5 kg bag and states that the latter two are not elemental P/K masses or an application rate.
Pass only when order, reporting bases, arithmetic and non-dose interpretation are all correct; otherwise targeted review and open retry.
